title: PromptEdit Shotlist Director (Claude skill for Seedance 2.0 shotlists)
summary: This is not a talking-head video but the full source of a packaged Claude skill that turns a script into a director's shotlist of AI-video generation prompts for Seedance 2.0. Its substance is a set of hard rules for writing shot prompts for a video model that has no memory between generations: a single global 'Style Prefix' block prepended verbatim to every prompt, an absolute ban on referential language ('same as before', 'still at the train station') because each prompt is the model's entire universe, a ground-truth rule that forbids inventing any appearance or location detail not supplied by the script or a reference image (and forbids describing a character at all when a reference image exists — @handle only), per-prompt sizing to the model's fixed clip length so no clip ends in dead air, dramatic rather than efficient allocation of shots, geo-spatial blocking, lens/height/movement camera language, and acting direction written as observable physical behaviour instead of emotion labels. It also specifies the deliverable as a self-contained HTML shotlist with per-scene checkboxes persisted in localStorage that the model rewrites on every revision rather than answering in chat.
recencySignals: Seedance 2.0 as the target video model; Claude skill format with YAML name/description frontmatter and /mnt/user-data/outputs; localStorage HTML artifact; published 2026. Current-era platform mechanics.

tactics.claim: Write a single global 'Style Prefix' block — photorealism level, lighting doctrine, colour ratio, lens and shutter, skin detail, acting register, physics, continuity, frame rate, audio rules — and prepend it verbatim to every single shot prompt in the project, then reinforce it per shot with the specific lighting geometry of that frame (where the window is, what the haze is doing, which colour dominates).
tactics.mechanism: A video model has no project-level memory, so the only way a sequence of separately generated clips shares one look is if the same look instruction is physically present in each prompt. Keeping it as one locked block means every prompt is copy-paste-ready standalone with no reassembly, and the per-shot lighting specifics tell the model where to actually place the rim light rather than leaving it to chance.
tactics.evidence: Assertion only — presented as the skill's law, with a full default prefix supplied.

rscFit.reasoning: He produces his own short-form video and AI-assisted ads solo, and the existing skills already cover writing scene prompts from a fixed template; this adds the missing cross-shot consistency mechanism, which is exactly the failure mode when a 30-second deodorant ad is assembled from six separately generated clips. Current-era platform mechanics (2026), so no age discount.

tactics.claim: Never write referential language in any field of a generation prompt — 'same as last shot', 'still at the train station', 'as established earlier', 'continues from the previous prompt' — and instead restate the location, setting, time of day and every character's physical state in full, explicit language in every prompt, even when it repeats the previous prompt word for word.
tactics.mechanism: Each generation is rendered in complete isolation with no memory of the script or of other prompts, so a phrase that only makes sense to someone who read a different prompt cannot be resolved and will be rendered wrong or ignored. The test is: if a phrase depends on another prompt for meaning, it is broken. Repetition across 1a/1b/1c is mandatory, not wasteful.
tactics.evidence: Assertion only, but with an explicit forbidden-phrase list, a stated test, and two worked examples.

rscFit.reasoning: This is the single most common reason a multi-clip AI ad falls apart mid-sequence, and he assembles ads from multiple generations himself today. It generalises beyond video to any isolated-generation prompt, including the image frames used for listing and ad statics. Runnable at $30/day with no extra tooling.

tactics.claim: Before writing any prompt, inventory exactly what you have — which characters and locations have uploaded reference images, and what the script explicitly states — and treat that inventory as a hard boundary: a character with a reference image is referred to by @handle only with no appearance description at all, a character without one gets only the details the script literally states, and any missing detail stays missing rather than being filled in for vividness.
tactics.mechanism: A text appearance description written alongside a reference image can contradict the image, so the image must be the sole source of truth for how a subject looks. Inventing detail to make a prompt read better produces a render that does not match the real subject or product. A sparse accurate prompt is correct; a vivid invented one is wrong.
tactics.evidence: Two contrasting worked examples (Case A with reference images, Case B without) showing precisely which details are absent from the second.

rscFit.reasoning: He grounds generations in real photos of the actual product and of himself, so the rule that the reference image wins and no text description competes with it directly protects against renders that misrepresent a real pack or a real face — the exact defect the existing hallucination-audit claim catches after the fact, prevented here before the generation is spent.

tactics.claim: Write acting direction as observable physical behaviour rather than emotion labels — not 'she looks sad' but 'her eyes drop to the table, jaw tightens, she swallows once before answering'; not 'he's angry' but 'knuckles whiten on the glass, breath shortens, eyes never leave hers' — express carried-over emotion as how it looks right now ('her hands haven't stopped shaking'), and default to restraint, because a whispered line outperforms a screamed one in most cases.
tactics.mechanism: A model can render a described physical action but has to guess at an emotion label, so naming the behaviour is the only way to control the performance. Expressing emotional state as present-tense visible fact also keeps the prompt standalone. Restraint reads as real; big emotion only when the moment earns it.
tactics.evidence: Assertion with six before/after rewrite pairs.

rscFit.reasoning: Directly usable twice over: in his AI video prompts and in directing his own on-camera delivery, where 'look relieved' is unfilmable and 'exhale, shoulders drop, half-smile' is. Durable craft principle, so age is irrelevant, and it needs nothing but a prompt field.

tactics.claim: Block every shot geo-spatially: state where each subject and prop sits relative to the location and to each other in literal terms — 'she sits across from him at the diner booth, knees touching under the table', 'the space between them is roughly twelve feet', 'he stops in the doorway six feet behind her' — rather than 'they sit and talk'.
tactics.mechanism: Explicit spatial relations are what let the model render a coherent, consistent space; without them it reinvents the geometry of the room on every generation and the cuts stop matching.
tactics.evidence: Assertion plus the worked example, which states distances and positions in every Scene block.

tactics.claim: Size every prompt to the model's fixed clip length and write enough cuts and acting beats to fill it, because the model renders a fixed-length clip and an under-written prompt ends in dead air; a 12-second moment still gets a full-length prompt filled with the breath, the look and the held silence after the line.
tactics.mechanism: The generator produces a clip of fixed duration regardless of how much you described, so the only way to avoid wasted seconds at the tail is to design the beats to occupy the whole window — either one long held shot that carries the moment or a rapid multi-cut sequence, whichever the action calls for.

tactics.claim: Allocate shots by dramatic weight rather than by script length — give a heavy line its own prompt, give a reveal a single sustained close-up and refuse to undercut it with extra cuts, split a confession so it has air, compress an action sequence into short cuts; 'don't pack the script efficiently, pack it dramatically'.
tactics.mechanism: Runtime is the only currency you have for emphasis, so spending it in proportion to the words rather than in proportion to the drama flattens the moment the piece exists to deliver.

rscFit.reasoning: Translates honestly to his 30-second ads: the mechanism claim or the result reveal gets its own held shot while the setup compresses, rather than every line getting equal screen time. Durable craft principle, so age is irrelevant.
